database-systems-map.code:
-- Database Systems Map: the CDC freshness gap
--
-- The store's SOURCE OF TRUTH is products_primary (the OLTP Postgres primary).
-- Every write lands here first, atomically.
--
-- The catalog page does NOT read the primary. It reads search_index, a DERIVED
-- store kept up to date by Change-Data-Capture (CDC). CDC is asynchronous, so a
-- brand-new product exists in the primary but is QUERY-INVISIBLE until it is
-- indexed. That lag is the "suspect edge" from the lesson.
--
-- products 3 and 5 were written to the primary but have not been indexed yet.

CREATE TABLE products_primary (
  product_id  INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name        TEXT NOT NULL,
  price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL,
  created_at  TEXT NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO products_primary (product_id, name, price_cents, created_at) VALUES
  (1, 'Cedar Desk',   24900, '2026-06-01T09:00:00Z'),
  (2, 'Oak Shelf',    13500, '2026-06-02T11:30:00Z'),
  (3, 'Maple Stool',   6900, '2026-06-03T08:15:00Z'),
  (4, 'Walnut Bench', 18800, '2026-06-04T14:45:00Z'),
  (5, 'Birch Lamp',    4200, '2026-06-05T10:05:00Z');

-- The derived, eventually-consistent read store the catalog actually queries.
CREATE TABLE search_index (
  product_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  indexed_at TEXT NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO search_index (product_id, indexed_at) VALUES
  (1, '2026-06-01T09:00:07Z'),
  (2, '2026-06-02T11:30:05Z'),
  (4, '2026-06-04T14:45:09Z');

-- TODO: Select product_id and name for every product that exists in
-- products_primary but is MISSING from search_index (the freshness-gap rows).
-- Return columns named product_id and name, ordered by product_id ascending.

SELECT p.product_id, p.name
FROM products_primary p
LEFT JOIN search_index s ON s.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE s.product_id IS NULL
ORDER BY p.product_id;

entities-relationships.code:
-- Entities & Relationships lab
-- Schema models: a customer places many orders (1-to-many),
-- and each order contains many products via order_items (many-to-many).
-- The order_items table is the JOIN (junction) table linking orders <-> products,
-- carrying its own attribute: quantity.

CREATE TABLE customers (
  id     INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  email  TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
);

CREATE TABLE products (
  id     INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name   TEXT NOT NULL,
  price  INTEGER NOT NULL          -- price in whole dollars
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id           INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id)
);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id    INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id),
  product_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id),
  quantity    INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)   -- composite key: one line per product per order
);

INSERT INTO customers (id, email) VALUES
  (1, 'ada@example.com'),
  (2, 'grace@example.com'),
  (3, 'linus@example.com');   -- linus has no orders

INSERT INTO products (id, name, price) VALUES
  (1, 'Keyboard', 80),
  (2, 'Mouse', 25),
  (3, 'Monitor', 200);

INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id) VALUES
  (1, 1),   -- ada
  (2, 1),   -- ada
  (3, 2);   -- grace

INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id, quantity) VALUES
  (1, 1, 1),   -- order 1: 1 Keyboard  (80)
  (1, 2, 2),   -- order 1: 2 Mouse     (50)
  (2, 3, 1),   -- order 2: 1 Monitor   (200)
  (3, 2, 4);   -- order 3: 4 Mouse     (100)

-- TODO: Return the email and total_spent for every customer who has placed
-- at least one order. total_spent = SUM(quantity * price) across all their
-- order items. Traverse customers -> orders -> order_items -> products.
-- Columns (exactly): email, total_spent
-- Order by total_spent DESC, then email ASC.
-- Write your SELECT below:

SELECT c.email, SUM(oi.quantity * p.price) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o        ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items oi  ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p      ON p.id = oi.product_id
GROUP BY c.id, c.email
ORDER BY total_spent DESC, c.email ASC;

-- Normalized schema (3NF): email lives ONCE, on customers.
-- orders no longer carries a duplicated customer_email copy;
-- the foreign key guards the invariant, and reads JOIN to get email.

CREATE TABLE customers (
  id    INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name  TEXT NOT NULL,
  email TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),  -- FK: single source of truth
  total       INTEGER NOT NULL,
  created_at  TEXT NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO customers (id, name, email) VALUES
  (1, 'Ada Lovelace',   'ada@calc.io'),
  (2, 'Grace Hopper',   'grace@navy.mil'),
  (3, 'Alan Turing',    'alan@bletchley.uk');

INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, total, created_at) VALUES
  (101, 1, 120, '2026-01-04'),
  (102, 2,  40, '2026-01-05'),
  (103, 1,  60, '2026-01-06'),
  (104, 3, 200, '2026-01-07'),
  (105, 2,  75, '2026-01-08');

-- TODO: Because email is no longer duplicated on orders, you must JOIN
-- orders to customers to read it. Return three columns aliased exactly:
--   name  | email | spent
-- where spent is the SUM of that customer's order totals.
-- Order by spent DESC, then name ASC. Write your query below.

SELECT c.name, c.email, SUM(o.total) AS spent
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name, c.email
ORDER BY spent DESC, c.name ASC;

constraints-invariants.code:
-- Enforced invariants live in `accounts`:
--   INV-1  email is NOT NULL and UNIQUE (one account per email)
--   INV-2  balance CHECK (balance >= 0)  -- money can never go negative
CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  email   TEXT    NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  balance INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (balance >= 0)
);

INSERT INTO accounts (id, email, balance) VALUES
  (1, 'ada@corp.io',    120),
  (2, 'grace@corp.io',   45),
  (3, 'linus@corp.io',    0);

-- A staging table of proposed new rows an import wants to add.
-- None of these have been inserted into `accounts` yet.
CREATE TABLE candidate_accounts (
  cand_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  email   TEXT,
  balance INTEGER
);

INSERT INTO candidate_accounts (cand_id, email, balance) VALUES
  (1, 'mike@corp.io',   50),    -- ok
  (2, 'ada@corp.io',    10),    -- violates INV-1 (duplicate email)
  (3, NULL,             30),    -- violates INV-1 (null email)
  (4, 'ken@corp.io',   -5),     -- violates INV-2 (negative balance)
  (5, 'dennis@corp.io', 75);    -- ok

-- TODO: Report every candidate that would VIOLATE an enforced invariant if it
-- were inserted into `accounts`. Output columns: cand_id, reason.
-- Use reason = 'null_email'        when the email is NULL,
--             'negative_balance'  when balance < 0,
--             'duplicate_email'   when the email already exists in accounts.
-- Each violating row here breaks exactly one invariant. Order by cand_id ascending.
--
-- Write your SELECT below:

SELECT cand_id,
       CASE
         WHEN email IS NULL THEN 'null_email'
         WHEN balance < 0 THEN 'negative_balance'
         WHEN email IN (SELECT email FROM accounts) THEN 'duplicate_email'
       END AS reason
FROM candidate_accounts
WHERE email IS NULL
   OR balance < 0
   OR email IN (SELECT email FROM accounts)
ORDER BY cand_id;

-- Access pattern lab: serve the "open orders for a tenant, newest first" read.
--
-- The team added this index to serve one hot query:
--   CREATE INDEX idx_orders_tenant_status_created
--     ON orders (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC);
-- Equality on (tenant_id, status) pins a slice, then created_at gives sorted order.
--
-- Fixed seed data (do not change):
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id   INTEGER NOT NULL,
  status      TEXT NOT NULL,
  total       INTEGER NOT NULL,
  created_at  TEXT NOT NULL
);

  (1, 42, 'open',      120, '2026-06-01 09:00:00'),
  (2, 42, 'closed',    300, '2026-06-02 09:00:00'),
  (3, 42, 'open',      250, '2026-06-05 14:30:00'),
  (4, 42, 'open',      180, '2026-06-04 11:15:00'),
  (5, 99, 'open',      500, '2026-06-06 08:00:00'),
  (6, 42, 'cancelled',  90, '2026-06-03 10:00:00'),
  (7, 42, 'open',      410, '2026-06-06 16:45:00'),
  (8, 99, 'closed',    220, '2026-06-05 12:00:00');

-- TODO: Write the query this index serves.
-- Return id and total for tenant_id = 42 with status = 'open',
-- ordered by created_at newest-first, limited to the 3 most recent.

query-design-joins.code:
-- Scenario: a small store. Each customer has orders; each order has line items.
-- Joining customers -> orders -> line_items changes the grain to one row PER ITEM,
-- so SUM(order_total) double/triple-counts multi-item orders.
--
-- Goal: return one row per customer with:
--   name       = customer name
--   revenue    = correct SUM of order_total (each order counted ONCE)
--   item_count = total number of line items across the customer's orders
-- Order by revenue DESC, then name ASC.

CREATE TABLE customers (
  id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  order_total INTEGER NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE line_items (
  id       INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  order_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  sku      TEXT NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO customers (id, name) VALUES
  (1, 'Ada'),
  (2, 'Grace'),
  (3, 'Linus');

INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, order_total) VALUES
  (10, 1, 200),   -- Ada, 3 items
  (11, 1, 150),   -- Ada, 1 item
  (12, 2, 300),   -- Grace, 2 items
  (13, 3,  90);   -- Linus, 1 item

INSERT INTO line_items (id, order_id, sku) VALUES
  (100, 10, 'A'),
  (101, 10, 'B'),
  (102, 10, 'C'),
  (103, 11, 'D'),
  (104, 12, 'E'),
  (105, 12, 'F'),
  (106, 13, 'G');

-- TODO: Write ONE SELECT below.
-- Hint: pre-aggregate line_items to ORDER grain in a CTE (one row per order,
-- with its item_count), THEN join customers -> orders -> that rollup.
-- Columns must be named exactly: name, revenue, item_count.
-- ORDER BY revenue DESC, name ASC.

WITH item_rollup AS (
  SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS item_count
  FROM line_items
  GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT c.name,
       SUM(o.order_total) AS revenue,
       SUM(ir.item_count) AS item_count
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o       ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN item_rollup ir ON ir.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY revenue DESC, c.name ASC;

isolation-concurrency.code:
-- Isolation & concurrency: hunting the lost-update anomaly
--
-- A lost update happens when two sessions each do read-modify-write on the
-- same row: they BOTH read the same starting qty, both subtract, and the
-- second COMMIT silently overwrites the first. The lesson's fix was to take
-- a row lock on read (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) so the second session blocks.
--
-- This table is the post-mortem audit log. Each row is one committed
-- transaction: which item it touched, which session did it, the qty it READ
-- at BEGIN, and the qty it WROTE at COMMIT. The fingerprint of a lost update
-- is two or more committed writes to the SAME item that READ the SAME qty --
-- proof they ran against the same snapshot instead of being serialized.

CREATE TABLE audit_log (
  id           INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  item_id      INTEGER NOT NULL,
  session      TEXT    NOT NULL,
  qty_read     INTEGER NOT NULL,  -- value the txn read at BEGIN
  qty_written  INTEGER NOT NULL,  -- value the txn wrote at COMMIT
  committed_at TEXT    NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO audit_log (id, item_id, session, qty_read, qty_written, committed_at) VALUES
  (1, 7,  'A', 5, 4, '2026-06-01T09:00:01'),  -- A reads 5
  (2, 7,  'B', 5, 4, '2026-06-01T09:00:02'),  -- B ALSO read 5 -> lost update
  (3, 12, 'A', 8, 7, '2026-06-01T09:05:00'),  -- read 8...
  (4, 12, 'A', 7, 6, '2026-06-01T09:05:03'),  -- then read 7: serialized, safe
  (5, 20, 'A', 3, 2, '2026-06-01T09:10:00'),  -- read 3...
  (6, 20, 'B', 2, 1, '2026-06-01T09:10:04'),  -- read 2: serialized, safe
  (7, 31, 'A', 9, 8, '2026-06-01T09:20:00'),  -- A reads 9
  (8, 31, 'B', 9, 8, '2026-06-01T09:20:01'),  -- B read 9
  (9, 31, 'C', 9, 8, '2026-06-01T09:20:02');  -- C read 9 -> three-way lost update

-- TODO: Return one row per (item_id, shared read value) where MORE THAN ONE
-- session committed a write against that same read value. Report three columns:
--   item_id            -- the affected item
--   overlapping_writes -- how many committed writes collided on that read value
--   shared_read        -- the qty they all read (use MIN(qty_read))
-- Group by item_id and qty_read, keep only groups with COUNT(*) > 1,
-- and ORDER BY item_id so the output is deterministic.
--
-- Write your SELECT below:

SELECT item_id,
       COUNT(*) AS overlapping_writes,
       MIN(qty_read) AS shared_read
FROM audit_log
GROUP BY item_id, qty_read
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY item_id;

-- Expand-contract migration, mid-flight.

-- to orders. Some rows were backfilled by an earlier batch; the rest are
-- still NULL. Your job is Phase 2: the BACKFILL.

  customer      text    NOT NULL,

  (2, 'Alan Turing',     'alan@bombe.uk',    NULL),           -- still needs backfill
  (3, 'Grace Hopper',    'grace@navy.mil',   NULL),           -- still needs backfill
  (4, 'Katherine J.',    'kat@nasa.gov',     'kat@nasa.gov'), -- already backfilled
  (5, 'Edsger Dijkstra', 'edsger@ewd.nl',    NULL);           -- still needs backfill

-- Copy email into contact_email, but ONLY for rows that still need it.
-- It must be IDEMPOTENT: re-running it must not touch already-backfilled
-- rows. (Guard on contact_email IS NULL, exactly as the lesson showed.)

query-plans-performance.code:
-- Scenario: an "orders" table. The slow query in the lesson scanned every row
-- filtering on status = 'open' AND a recent created_at range. The fix was a
-- PARTIAL index -- ONE key column (created_at), restricted to just the rows we
-- actually query:
--
--   CREATE INDEX idx_orders_open_recent
--     ON orders (created_at)
--     WHERE status = 'open';
--
-- It is partial, not composite. A composite index would be ON (status, created_at)
-- and would store a status value that is the same in every row it contains.
-- Partial excludes the column instead of indexing it.

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  status      TEXT    NOT NULL,
  total       INTEGER NOT NULL,
  created_at  TEXT    NOT NULL   -- ISO date, sorts lexicographically
);

INSERT INTO orders (id, status, total, created_at) VALUES

  (5,  'cancelled', 200, '2026-06-15'),
  (6,  'open',       75, '2026-05-20'),
  (7,  'shipped',   410, '2026-06-16'),
  (8,  'open',      260, '2026-06-16'),
  (9,  'open',      130, '2026-06-17'),
  (10, 'cancelled',  99, '2026-06-12');

CREATE INDEX idx_orders_open_recent
  ON orders (created_at)
  WHERE status = 'open';

-- TODO 1 -- the deliverable: OPEN orders created on or after '2026-06-13'.
SELECT id, total
FROM orders

ORDER BY created_at, id;

-- An OrderRepository hides storage details from callers.
-- The physical table uses `amount_cents`, but the domain object

--        id           -> orderId
--        customer_id  -> customerId
--        amount_cents -> amountCents
--        status       -> status
--   3. Order the rows by orderId so results are deterministic.

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id           TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id  TEXT NOT NULL,
  amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL,
  status       TEXT NOT NULL
);

data-quality-checks.code:
-- Data-quality contract lab · SQLite (sql.js), runs fresh in your browser.
-- In the lesson, a PASSING check returns ZERO rows; any returned row is a violation to fix.
-- Here we INVERT that: your job is to LIST the violating orders so a human can triage them.

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INTEGER,
  amount      REAL,
  status      TEXT,
  shipped_at  TEXT      -- ISO date, or NULL if not yet shipped
);

INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, amount, status, shipped_at) VALUES
  (1, 100,  49.99, 'shipped',    '2026-06-01'),  -- clean
  (2, 101,  -5.00, 'refunded',    NULL),          -- BAD: amount < 0
  (3, 102, 120.00, 'shipped',     NULL),          -- BAD: shipped but no shipped_at
  (4, 103,   0.00, 'pending',     NULL),          -- clean (0 is allowed)
  (5, 104, -19.50, 'shipped',     NULL),          -- BAD: amount < 0 AND shipped w/o date
  (6, 105,  75.25, 'shipped',    '2026-06-10'),   -- clean
  (7, 106,  10.00, 'pending',     NULL);          -- clean

-- DOMAIN INVARIANT: amount must be >= 0, and status='shipped' implies shipped_at IS NOT NULL.
-- TODO: SELECT the id of every order that VIOLATES the invariant.
-- Return one column named "id", ordered by id ascending.

SELECT id
FROM orders
WHERE amount < 0
   OR (status = 'shipped' AND shipped_at IS NULL)
ORDER BY id;

backup-restore-retention.code:
-- Scenario: nightly disaster-recovery drills.
-- Every night a backup of the production `orders` table is restored into a
-- scratch DB and verified. A drill PASSES only if:
--   (1) restored_rows == source_rows for that day  (zero-drift parity), AND
--   (2) elapsed restore time <= the RTO target (30 minutes).
--
-- source_rows = the true production row count captured at backup time.
-- restored_rows / elapsed_min = what the restore drill actually measured.

CREATE TABLE restore_drills (
  drill_date     TEXT PRIMARY KEY,  -- YYYY-MM-DD
  source_rows    INTEGER NOT NULL,  -- prod count at backup time
  restored_rows  INTEGER NOT NULL,  -- rows found after pg_restore
  elapsed_min    INTEGER NOT NULL   -- restore + verify wall-clock minutes
);

INSERT INTO restore_drills (drill_date, source_rows, restored_rows, elapsed_min) VALUES
  ('2026-06-13', 480200, 480200, 22),  -- clean
  ('2026-06-14', 481050, 481050, 41),  -- clean rows but too slow (RTO breach)
  ('2026-06-15', 482310, 482297, 19),  -- fast but 13 rows short (drift)
  ('2026-06-16', 483500, 483500, 30),  -- clean, exactly at the RTO limit
  ('2026-06-17', 484900, 484915, 28);  -- extra 15 rows (drift, wrong direction)

-- RTO target is 30 minutes. Parity means restored_rows = source_rows.
-- TODO: return one row per drill (ordered by drill_date) with columns:
--   drill_date,
--   row_delta  = restored_rows - source_rows,
--   elapsed_min,
--   verdict    = 'PASS' when parity AND elapsed_min <= 30, else 'FAIL'

SELECT drill_date,
       restored_rows - source_rows AS row_delta,
       elapsed_min,
       CASE WHEN restored_rows = source_rows AND elapsed_min <= 30
            THEN 'PASS' ELSE 'FAIL' END AS verdict
FROM restore_drills
ORDER BY drill_date;

security-privacy-compliance.code:
-- Security, privacy & compliance in the database itself.
--
-- In Postgres the lesson enforced two rules structurally:
--   * TENANT ISOLATION  -> a row-level-security policy:  tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')
--   * ERASURE / SOFT DELETE -> a partial index over live rows only:  WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
--
-- SQLite has no RLS, so here you write the query a correctly-scoped
-- app role would run: restrict to one tenant AND exclude erased rows.

CREATE TABLE users (
  id           INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id    TEXT    NOT NULL,
  email        TEXT    NOT NULL,
  ssn_last4    TEXT,          -- would be encrypted at the boundary in prod
  deleted_at   TEXT           -- NULL = live; a timestamp = erased (soft-deleted)
);

INSERT INTO users (id, tenant_id, email, ssn_last4, deleted_at) VALUES
  (1, 'acme',   'ada@acme.io',    '1234', NULL),
  (2, 'acme',   'grace@acme.io',  '5678', NULL),

  (6, 'acme',   'linus@acme.io',  '2222', NULL);

caching-read-models.code:
-- SCENARIO: A dashboard reads a derived "read model" (daily_revenue),
-- never SUM(orders) live. daily_revenue is a query-shaped copy that must be
-- REBUILT from the source of truth. The invalidation rule: only 'settled'
-- orders count toward revenue (pending/refunded are excluded).

-- Source of truth
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id           INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  order_date   TEXT    NOT NULL,
  amount_cents INTEGER NOT NULL,
  status       TEXT    NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO orders (id, order_date, amount_cents, status) VALUES
  (1, '2026-06-01', 1200, 'settled'),
  (2, '2026-06-01',  800, 'settled'),
  (3, '2026-06-01',  500, 'pending'),
  (4, '2026-06-02', 3000, 'settled'),
  (5, '2026-06-02',  450, 'refunded'),
  (6, '2026-06-02', 2000, 'settled'),
  (7, '2026-06-03',  999, 'pending'),
  (8, '2026-06-03', 1500, 'settled'),
  (9, '2026-06-01',  300, 'refunded');

-- The read model (starts empty; you must refresh it from orders)
CREATE TABLE daily_revenue (
  order_date    TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  revenue_cents INTEGER NOT NULL,
  order_count   INTEGER NOT NULL
);

-- TODO 1: Refresh/rebuild the read model. INSERT one row per order_date into
--   daily_revenue holding SUM(amount_cents) AS revenue_cents and COUNT(*) AS
--   order_count, counting ONLY status = 'settled' orders, grouped by order_date.

-- TODO 2: Serve the dashboard by reading the read model:
--   SELECT order_date, revenue_cents, order_count FROM daily_revenue
--   ORDER BY order_date.

INSERT INTO daily_revenue (order_date, revenue_cents, order_count)
SELECT order_date, SUM(amount_cents), COUNT(*)
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'settled'
GROUP BY order_date;

SELECT order_date, revenue_cents, order_count
FROM daily_revenue
ORDER BY order_date;

analytics-warehouse-boundaries.code:
-- Boundary: OLTP orders (source of truth) -> analytics.fct_orders (warehouse).
-- The warehouse has NO UNIQUE constraint on order_id, so CDC replays can land the
-- SAME order_id more than once. Each reload gets a fresh loaded_at. The row with the
-- greatest loaded_at is the current truth; older rows are stale soft-duplicates.
-- (This in-memory SQLite table stands in for analytics.fct_orders.)

CREATE TABLE fct_orders (
  order_id      INTEGER,   -- NOT unique: soft-duplicate tolerant
  customer_hash TEXT,
  total_cents   INTEGER,
  status        TEXT,
  ordered_at    TEXT,
  loaded_at     TEXT       -- later load = newer snapshot of that order_id
);

INSERT INTO fct_orders (order_id, customer_hash, total_cents, status, ordered_at, loaded_at) VALUES
  -- order 101: first loaded as 'pending', CDC replay later corrects it to 'completed' + new total
  (101, 'c_ada',  2000, 'pending',   '2024-01-02', '2024-01-02T06:00:00Z'),
  (101, 'c_ada',  2500, 'completed', '2024-01-02', '2024-01-03T06:00:00Z'),
  -- order 102: clean single load, completed
  (102, 'c_ada',  4000, 'completed', '2024-01-02', '2024-01-02T06:05:00Z'),
  -- order 103: replayed twice; final snapshot is 'refunded' (must NOT count)
  (103, 'c_bob',  9000, 'completed', '2024-01-02', '2024-01-02T06:10:00Z'),
  (103, 'c_bob',  9000, 'refunded',  '2024-01-02', '2024-01-04T06:10:00Z'),
  -- order 104: bob, completed, single load
  (104, 'c_bob',  1500, 'completed', '2024-01-03', '2024-01-03T06:00:00Z'),
  -- order 105: cid, only ever pending -> excluded by status
  (105, 'c_cid',  7000, 'pending',   '2024-01-03', '2024-01-03T06:00:00Z'),
  -- order 106: cid, replayed; stale row says completed 500, latest says completed 800
  (106, 'c_cid',   500, 'completed', '2024-01-03', '2024-01-03T06:00:00Z'),
  (106, 'c_cid',   800, 'completed', '2024-01-03', '2024-01-05T06:00:00Z');

-- TODO: Collapse each order_id to its LATEST-loaded row (greatest loaded_at),
-- keep only status = 'completed', then return each customer's total revenue in dollars.
-- Output columns: customer_hash, revenue_dollars  (revenue_dollars = SUM(total_cents)/100.0)
-- Order by customer_hash ascending.

WITH latest AS (
  SELECT order_id, MAX(loaded_at) AS max_loaded
  FROM fct_orders
  GROUP BY order_id
),
current_rows AS (
  SELECT f.*
  FROM fct_orders f
  JOIN latest l ON l.order_id = f.order_id AND l.max_loaded = f.loaded_at
)
SELECT customer_hash,
       SUM(total_cents) / 100.0 AS revenue_dollars
FROM current_rows
WHERE status = 'completed'
GROUP BY customer_hash
ORDER BY customer_hash;

observability-incidents.code:
-- Incident triage: a deploy at 14:00 made the app slow.
-- You have two observability tables captured from the database.

-- query_stats: one row per statement the DB executed a lot.
--   filter_column = the column the statement filters on (like pg_stat_statements normalized text)
--   mean_ms_before / mean_ms_after = mean execution time before vs after the deploy
CREATE TABLE query_stats (
  statement       TEXT NOT NULL,
  table_name      TEXT NOT NULL,
  filter_column   TEXT NOT NULL,
  calls           INTEGER NOT NULL,
  mean_ms_before  REAL NOT NULL,
  mean_ms_after   REAL NOT NULL
);

-- indexes: the index catalog AFTER the deploy (which indexes still exist).
CREATE TABLE indexes (
  table_name    TEXT NOT NULL,
  indexed_column TEXT NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO query_stats (statement, table_name, filter_column, calls, mean_ms_before, mean_ms_after) VALUES
  ('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = $1',   'orders',   'customer_id',  90000, 3.0,   842.0),
  ('SELECT * FROM sessions WHERE token = $1',       'sessions', 'token',        50000, 2.5,   2.7),
  ('SELECT * FROM shipments WHERE order_id = $1',    'shipments','order_id',     12000, 4.0,   611.0),
  ('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1',           'users',    'email',        8000,  1.8,   1.9),
  ('SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE account_id = $1',   'invoices', 'account_id',   3000,  5.0,   9.0);

-- indexes remaining after the deploy (customer_id and order_id indexes were dropped):
INSERT INTO indexes (table_name, indexed_column) VALUES
  ('sessions', 'token'),
  ('users',    'email'),
  ('invoices', 'account_id');

-- TODO:
-- Report every statement that REGRESSED after the deploy
-- (mean_ms_after is at least 10x mean_ms_before) AND whose filter_column
-- has NO matching index in the `indexes` catalog for its table.
-- Return columns: table_name, filter_column, mean_ms_after
-- Order by mean_ms_after descending.

SELECT q.table_name, q.filter_column, q.mean_ms_after
FROM query_stats q
LEFT JOIN indexes i
  ON i.table_name = q.table_name
 AND i.indexed_column = q.filter_column
WHERE q.mean_ms_after >= 10 * q.mean_ms_before
  AND i.table_name IS NULL
ORDER BY q.mean_ms_after DESC;

-- Scenario: the orders table already exists with data, but has no status column.
-- Apply a SAFE forward migration (the pattern from the lesson):
--   1. Add the new column as NULLABLE  (no full-table rewrite/lock)
--   2. Backfill existing rows to a default value BEFORE relying on it
--   3. Reclassify the rows that need a different status
-- Then prove the new column works by summarizing orders per status.

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id       INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  customer TEXT NOT NULL,
  amount   INTEGER NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO orders (id, customer, amount) VALUES
  (1, 'Ada',   120),
  (2, 'Grace', 80),
  (3, 'Ada',   200),
  (4, 'Linus', 50),
  (5, 'Grace', 300);

-- ============================================================
-- TODO: Complete the migration below, then write the summary query.
--
-- Step 1: add a nullable TEXT column named `status`.
-- Step 2: backfill EVERY existing row so status = 'fulfilled' (the rows are
--         currently NULL because the column was just added).
-- Step 3: reclassify big orders — set status = 'pending' where amount >= 200.
--
-- Step 4: write the final SELECT so its result set is EXACTLY:
--         columns  -> status, order_count, revenue
--         where    order_count = COUNT(*) per status
--                  revenue     = SUM(amount) per status
--         GROUP BY status, and ORDER BY status so row order is deterministic.
-- ============================================================

-- Step 1:


-- Step 2:


-- Step 3:


-- Step 4 (final query — its output is checked):

ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN status TEXT;

UPDATE orders SET status = 'fulfilled';

UPDATE orders SET status = 'pending' WHERE amount >= 200;

       COUNT(*) AS order_count,
       SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM orders
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY status;

database-capstone.code:
-- Migration capstone: you are about to enforce a per-org, case-insensitive
-- unique-email invariant with a UNIQUE INDEX on (org_id, lower(email)).
-- Because that index is over an expression, Postgres will NOT let you promote
-- it into a table constraint (UNIQUE USING INDEX rejects expression indexes) --
-- the unique index itself is the enforcer. But before you build it, you MUST
-- prove no existing data already violates it, or the build fails mid-flight.
-- Write the "verify" query that lists each colliding group.

CREATE TABLE users (
  id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  org_id  INTEGER NOT NULL,
  email   TEXT    NOT NULL
);

INSERT INTO users (id, org_id, email) VALUES
  (1, 10, 'ada@acme.io'),
  (2, 10, 'grace@acme.io'),
  (3, 10, 'ADA@acme.io'),     -- collides with id 1 (same org, same email ignoring case)
  (4, 20, 'ada@acme.io'),     -- different org, so NOT a collision with id 1
  (5, 20, 'lin@beta.dev'),
  (6, 20, 'Lin@beta.dev'),    -- collides with id 5
  (7, 20, 'lin@BETA.dev'),    -- also collides with id 5
  (8, 30, 'sole@gamma.co');

-- TODO: Return one row per violating group.
-- Columns (in this order and with these names):
--   org_id, email_key, dup_count
-- where email_key is the lowercased email, and dup_count is how many rows
-- share that (org_id, email_key). Only include groups with more than one row.
-- Order by org_id, then email_key, so the output is deterministic.

SELECT org_id,
       lower(email) AS email_key,
       COUNT(*) AS dup_count
FROM users
GROUP BY org_id, lower(email)
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY org_id, email_key;
